newsitem.title: USA: IMF unlikely to sanction more cash for Russia now.
newsitem.headline: IMF unlikely to sanction more cash for Russia now.

text.p: An IMF mission will return to Moscow next week for further talks on Russia's cash-starved budget but it is not expected to sanction release of delayed funding for the nation, monetary sources said on Friday.

The sources, who declined to be named, said that the International Monetary Fund wants to make sure that Russia has succeeded in boosting depressed tax revenues before allowing Moscow to draw down further on its $10.2 billion IMF loan.
"The IMF will want to see a track record (of enhanced revenues)," one source said, adding, "It won't act (on the loan) until December at the earliest and it may take longer."

The IMF mission, which is expected to arrive in Moscow on Wednesday, will also discuss Russia's economic outlook with the nation's policymakers as part of its annual "Article Four" consultation -- a ritual it carries out with all its members.

Russian tax revenues collapsed in September, leading the IMF to decide last month to hold up payment of a $330 million loan tranche. Sources said September revenues were equal to only five to six percent of gross domestic product (gdp).
Russian officials have said that revenues have increased since then, boosted by an aggressive government campaign to get tax scofflaws to pay up.
"It remains to be seen how much tax collection has increased," one international monetary source said, adding, "Whatever the pick-up, it is from a very low base."

At best, the IMF will not know until December that revenues are on on upward trend. But even that might prove to be too soon, one source said. "I would expect a lot of trouble in the coming months," he added.

Besides being worried about low Russian tax revenues, the IMF has also voiced concern about Moscow's recent imposition of quotas on alchohol imports and its restrictions on treasury bill interest payments to foreign investors, sources said.
The quotas were imposed in response to a surge in imports of alchohol and vodka from Ukraine.
Under its loan agreement with the IMF, Russia is supposed to refrain from imposing quotas or similar restrictions on imports, although it can raise tariffs.
Sources said the IMF has also ruled that Russian restrictions on treasury bill interest payments to foreigners run counter to Moscow's obligations under Fund rules.
Those restrictions effectively mean that foreign investors have to wait for three months before they can repatriate interest payments on their treasury bill investments.

One source played down the significance of the alchohol import quotas and the treasury bill restrictions, saying that those differences could be settled quickly if the IMF was satisfied with the level of Russia's tax revenues.
